Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history.

**`git merge`** ties the two branches together with a new merge commit that has two parents. Existing commits are untouched.

```
Before:              After `git merge main` (on feature):

A---B---C  main      A---B---C-------M  feature
     \                    \         /
      D---E  feature       D---E---'
```

**`git rebase`** replays your commits one by one on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. History becomes a straight line, as if you had started your work from the latest commit.

```
Before:              After `git rebase main` (on feature):

A---B---C  main      A---B---C  main
     \                        \
      D---E  feature           D'---E'  feature
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserved as it happened, with branch points visible | Rewritten into a linear sequence |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Changed for every replayed commit |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Resolved per replayed commit, possibly several times |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No, because it rewrites commits others may have based work on |
| Undoing | Revert or reset the merge commit | Recover via `git reflog` |

**When to use which**

- **Rebase** to update your own local or unshared feature branch onto the latest `main`, or to tidy commits before opening a pull request (`git rebase -i`).
- **Merge** to bring a finished feature branch into a shared branch, or whenever the branch is already used by other people.

The main rule is not to rebase commits that others have already pulled. Their history will diverge from yours, and you would need a force push to publish the rewrite (use `--force-with-lease` if you do have to).

A common workflow combines both: rebase your feature branch onto `main` locally to keep it current, then merge it into `main` when it is done.
